blocks.text: **The problem.** You are given an array of positive integers `nums`. Return the **second largest distinct** value in it. If there isn't one — the array has a single element, or every element is the same — return `-1`.

blocks.alt: The array [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1]. 35 is marked as the largest and 34 as the second largest.

blocks.text: Example

blocks.code:
Input:  nums = [12, 35, 1, 10, 34, 1]
Output: 34

Input:  nums = [10, 5, 10]
Output: 5     the repeated 10 is still the largest, not the second largest

Input:  nums = [7, 7, 7]
Output: -1    nothing is smaller than the largest

blocks.text: Understanding the problem

The important word is **distinct**. In `[10, 5, 10]` the two 10s are the same value, so the second largest is 5 — not the second 10. A common bug is to sort the array and return the second-to-last element without checking for repeats.

This is a warm-up problem, but it teaches a habit you will use constantly: answering a question about the whole array in **one pass**, by carrying a small amount of information from element to element.
Approach 1: sort, then look from the top
Sort the values in descending order. The first value is the largest; walk forward until you meet a value that is different — that is the second largest.
Easy to get right, but sorting costs **O(n log n)** — we are putting every element in order just to learn about two of them.
Approach 2: one pass with two variables
Keep two numbers as you walk: `largest` and `second`. Each new value `x` falls into exactly one of three situations:

blocks.alt: Three rules for a new value x. If x is bigger than largest, the old largest becomes second and x becomes largest. If x is between second and largest, x becomes second. Otherwise x is ignored.
blocks.caption: When a new champion arrives, the old champion becomes the runner-up — it is never thrown away.

blocks.text: Notice the first rule: when a new largest value arrives, the old largest isn't lost — it **slides down** to become the second largest. Forgetting that step is the classic mistake.
Starting both variables at `-∞` means the very first element always takes the top spot, with no special case needed.
Dry run it yourself
Watch how `largest` and `second` change. Try `[10, 5, 10]` and `[7, 7, 7]` to see duplicates of the largest being skipped.
Code
In Java and C++ the trackers are `long` so that the "nothing yet" value can never collide with a real element.
Complexity

blocks.alt: Sorting: O(n log n) time, O(n) space. One pass: O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: One pass over the array with two variables: **O(n) time, O(1) space**.
Edge cases to test

items: **Second largest comes first** — `[9, 20, 3]`: the 9 must slide down when 20 arrives.

blocks.text: If the array could contain negative numbers, `-1` might be a real answer. In that case return something that can't be confused with one — `null` in JavaScript or `None` in Python.
Where this idea shows up again

Carrying "the best few so far" through a single pass is everywhere: the third largest value, the two numbers with the largest product, the smallest and largest together. When you need the top **k** for a large k, the same idea grows into a heap, which you'll meet in the Heap course.
